topic.title: Diwali has one film
topic.claim: At Diwali the family picks one film and every other release loses, because a festival ticket is a group decision and not a taste decision.
topic.behaviour: Families book seats together and choose what everyone, including the grandmother, can sit through. The weekend chart was lopsided: Ramayana took ₹174.00 crore of the top five's ₹252.75 crore net, and Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.
topic.mechanism: Theatres give shows to whatever fills the hall, and groups fill the hall for the film that is safe for all ages. A hit gets more screens, which makes it look even bigger.
topic.group: People who go to the movies with family at festival time
topic.moment: You wanted to see a different film this Diwali, but the family plan had one name on it.

turn.believed: The biggest film wins because it is the best film.
turn.actually: It wins because a group of different ages can agree on it, and screens then follow the crowd.

topic.feeling: Part of a crowd and slightly left out of your own choice
topic.villain: A screen-allocation system that rewards whatever fills the hall in the first weekend
topic.because: Exhibitors earn from full halls, so they move shows to the film families choose. The second-choice film loses its place even if people liked it.

proof.fact: Sacnilk puts the top five films at ₹252.75 crore net for the Diwali weekend, with Ramayana taking ₹174.00 Cr (69% of that). Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.

topic.payoff: A festival hit is the film the whole family could say yes to, not necessarily the one anyone loved most.
topic.send_to: The friend who always ends up watching what the family picks
real_details: Scene grew on both Saturday and Sunday, unlike the usual front-loaded star release
topic.news_peg: Sacnilk's Diwali weekend (November 6-8) box office report (2026-11-09)
topic.why_now: The Diwali weekend numbers have just come out.

score.why: A festival ticket is a group decision, not a taste decision. The box-office fact supports the argument instead of being the point.

violations: Hard failure 14, no relatability: the pattern is asserted more than shown. Beyond the WhatsApp group and the popcorn cousin, there is no third exact scene every reader has lived, such as the booking-app seat map, someone asking 'kaunsi dekhni hai?' or the grandmother asking what the film is about. Slides 3, 4 and 5 keep restating the rule ('group decision', 'sab dekh sakte hain', 'whatever survives') where a lived moment should carry it.
notes: Slides 3, 4 and 5 say the same thing three times: a ticket is a group decision, so the film must suit everyone, so 'sab dekh sakte hain' wins. Merge them into one slide with one concrete scene, such as the group chat where the grandmother's 'something clean' and the kids' 'not a serious one' cancel everything else. Delete 'Nobody gets their favourite' and the 'Whatever survives that vote' line, since they repeat the rule. Slide 3's why_swipe, 'what happens next?', is also filler.

Slide 1 states the whole answer ('the one the whole family could agree on'), and the last slide repeats it ('what your whole row could say yes to'), so the close adds nothing new. Keep the cover claim, but make the close a sting or a test the reader can run, for example: 'Next Diwali, count how many films were ever in the group chat.' Alternatively end on what the second-choice film actually loses: its showtimes.

Slides 6 to 8 need a clearer mechanism. Say plainly that the multiplex hands the 7pm Saturday slot to whichever film filled Friday, so the next film's audience arrives to find fewer shows. Slide 8's 'Their fans didn't vanish. Their showtimes did.' goes further than Sacnilk's 'lost screens' line, so soften it to what the source supports. Also say that 69% is the weekend share among the top five, so it is not read as national share.

Slide 9 ('It isn't bad taste...') and slide 10 both reassure the reader, which softens the sharp mood. Cut the 'six people happy in one row' line, which repeats slide 4. Spend the space on the feeling the topic names: part of the crowd, slightly left out of your own choice. A sensory beat would help here, such as the six-seat row, the shared popcorn tub that settles who sits where, or the cousin's phone lighting up when the film drags.

Slide 2 is the best slide because it shows the moment. Push it further with a second everyday beat, like the 'ok sab ready?' message arriving after the booking is already done, so the reader feels the decision was never theirs. That sets up the 'system, not family' turn without making the family the villain.

cover.headline: A Diwali hit is the film the [whole family agreed on]
cover.sub: Your pick lost before anyone booked a single ticket.

paragraphs:
A Diwali hit isn't the best film. It's the one the whole family could agree on.
Swipe to read →
slides.why_swipe: If it's not the best film, how does it win?

paragraphs: You had your own pick. Then the family WhatsApp group made the plan, and it had one name on it.
Your film became "baad mein OTT pe dekh lenge."
slides.why_swipe: Why does the group always land on that one film?

paragraphs: The group chat counts seats. Dadi has one condition: "koi maar-dhaad toh nahi hai na?" The kids veto anything "serious."
Your pick is the first to go. Then someone types "sab ko chalega?" and one name is left.
slides.why_swipe: And what do the theatres do with a row like that?

paragraphs: A hall earns from full seats, so its shows follow the crowd. The film families filled on Friday gets Saturday's shows.
Open the booking app on Saturday morning, and the show you wanted is often gone.
slides.why_swipe: Did that actually happen this weekend?

paragraphs: This Diwali weekend, Ramayana took 69% of what the top five films made. Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.
slides.why_swipe: So where were you in all this?

paragraphs: That one line put you in a seat, in a full hall that kept its shows. You helped build the hit.
slides.why_swipe: So what does the chart actually count?

paragraphs: Next festival, ask your row who picked the film first.
The chart doesn't count what anyone wanted. It counts what a whole row could sit through.

end.save: Read it again when the next festival box office numbers come out.
end.send: Send to the friend who always ends up watching whatever the family picks.
end.promise: How Indian choices really get made.

draft.caption: Most of us helped make this Diwali's biggest hit without ever picking it.
draft.alt_text: A text carousel of seven slides arguing that a Diwali box office hit is the film a whole family can agree on, not necessarily the best one. The family WhatsApp group makes the plan and the reader's pick becomes a 'later on OTT' plan. In the group chat, seats get counted, the grandmother asks if there's any violence, the kids veto anything serious, the reader's pick goes first, and someone asks 'will it work for everyone?'. Halls earn from full seats, so shows follow the crowd, and on Saturday morning the show you wanted is often gone. It cites Sacnilk: Ramayana took 69% of the top five films' Diwali weekend total, and Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens. The reader said 'okay, fine', helped build the hit, but didn't pick it. It ends by suggesting the reader ask their row who picked the film first, because the chart counts what a whole row could sit through, not what anyone wanted.

claims.text: Ramayana took 69% of the top five films' net collections over the Diwali weekend.
Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.
